scope: 18 existing original mock-eligible AQA Chemistry short cards: enthalpy/Born–Haber, gas Kp, Gibbs thermodynamics, and titration uncertainties.
safeguards: Only exact original IDs/front/back, Chemistry, AS or A2, mock-eligible active cards are patched.
Preserve earlier accepted/rejected variants; do not rewrite any original prompt, answer or progress ID.
These are concise one-fact cards; complete Born–Haber cycles and multi-step calculations remain exam questions.
Testing exact answers and curated wrong concepts does not certify all unfamiliar wording or complete specification coverage.
Saved progress, XP, cloud sync and original application questions are untouched.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalBack: The enthalpy change when 1 mole of gaseous atoms forms from an element in its standard state.
accept: Forming one mole of gaseous atoms from an element in its standard state.
reject: One mole of gaseous ions is formed by removing electrons from atoms.
One mole of solid ionic compound is formed from gaseous ions.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalBack: The enthalpy change when 1 mole of gaseous ions becomes hydrated, forming aqueous ions.
accept: One mole of gaseous ions becomes aqueous hydrated ions.
reject: An ionic solid separates into gaseous ions.
A compound forms from its elements in their standard states.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalBack: The enthalpy change when 1 mole of a solid ionic compound is formed from its constituent gaseous ions.
accept: One mole of ionic solid forms from its constituent gaseous ions.
reject: One mole of ionic solid becomes separate gaseous ions.
One mole of gaseous atoms forms from its element in the standard state.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalBack: The enthalpy change when 1 mole of solute dissolves in enough solvent to form an infinitely dilute solution.
accept: An enthalpy change as one mole of solute dissolves to make an infinitely dilute solution.
reject: One mole of gas ions becomes hydrated in aqueous solution, with no solid solute dissolved.
One mole of solute leaves an aqueous solution as a gas.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalBack: The enthalpy change when 1 mole of compound forms from its constituent elements in their standard states under standard conditions.
accept: One mole of compound forms from its elements in standard states at standard conditions.
reject: One mole of compound completely burns in oxygen at standard conditions.
An ionic lattice forms from separate gaseous ions only.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: In a Born–Haber cycle, define first ionisation energy.
rows.originalBack: Energy required to remove 1 mole of electrons from 1 mole of gaseous atoms, forming gaseous 1+ ions.
accept: Removing one electron from each atom in one mole of gaseous atoms to produce gaseous 1+ ions.
reject: Removing an electron from each gaseous 1+ ion to form gaseous 2+ ions.
Adding one electron to each neutral gaseous atom to make a gaseous anion.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalBack: A giant 3D repeating arrangement of oppositely charged ions held by electrostatic attractions.
accept: A regular, repeating giant 3D array of oppositely charged ions held by electrostatic attraction.
reject: Separate neutral molecules held together by only London forces.
A random collection of ions with no electrostatic forces between them.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalBack: The enthalpy change when 1 mole of gaseous 1− ions each gains an electron, forming gaseous 2− ions.
accept: One mole of gaseous 1− ions gains one mole of electrons to give gaseous 2− ions.
reject: One mole of neutral gaseous atoms gains electrons to form gaseous 1− ions.
One mole of gaseous 1− ions loses electrons and forms neutral atoms.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What goes into a Kp expression?
rows.originalBack: Partial pressures of gaseous equilibrium species, each raised to its stoichiometric coefficient.
accept: Equilibrium gas partial pressures, each raised to its balanced chemical equation coefficient.
reject: Initial amounts of gas before equilibrium, not equilibrium partial pressures.
The concentrations of solids and liquids must always appear in Kp.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: Define Kp for a homogeneous gaseous equilibrium.
rows.originalBack: The equilibrium constant expressed using the equilibrium partial pressures of the gases, at a fixed temperature.
accept: The equilibrium constant written using the equilibrium partial pressures of gases at a given temperature.
reject: The equilibrium constant calculated from initial gas pressures before equilibrium.
A value that must change when total pressure changes at constant temperature.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalBack: Kp = p(NH₃)² ÷ [p(N₂) × p(H₂)³]. Use equilibrium partial pressures.
accept: Ammonia equilibrium partial pressure squared over nitrogen equilibrium pressure times hydrogen equilibrium pressure cubed.
reject: N2 partial pressure times H2 cubed divided by NH3 squared.
Ammonia pressure over nitrogen pressure times hydrogen pressure, ignoring powers.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: When do the pressure units of Kp cancel?
rows.originalBack: When the total gaseous coefficients are equal on both sides, so Δn = 0.
accept: The pressure powers cancel when Δn is zero, with equal gaseous coefficient totals on both sides.
reject: Pressure units always cancel when there are unequal total gas coefficients.
Kp has no units whenever the pressure unit is kPa rather than Pa.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: How does increasing T affect ΔG when ΔS is positive versus negative?
rows.originalBack: For ΔS > 0, ΔG decreases (more favourable). For ΔS < 0, ΔG increases (less favourable).
accept: At fixed ΔH and ΔS, heating lowers ΔG for positive ΔS and raises ΔG for negative ΔS.
reject: Heating raises ΔG for positive entropy change and lowers ΔG for negative entropy change.
Changing temperature never changes ΔG even when ΔS is not zero.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: Why does negative ΔG not guarantee a rapid reaction?
rows.originalBack: ΔG predicts thermodynamic feasibility, not rate. A high activation energy can make the reaction very slow.
accept: A feasible reaction with negative ΔG can still be very slow if its activation energy is large.
reject: A negative ΔG always means the reaction is fast.
If ΔG is negative then activation energy must be zero.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: State the Gibbs free-energy equation and the unit rule.
rows.originalBack: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS. T in K; use matching energy units for ΔH and TΔS (convert J to kJ if needed).
accept: Delta G equals delta H minus T times delta S, with Kelvin temperature and consistent energy units.
reject: Delta G equals delta H plus T times delta S.
Use degrees Celsius for T and mixed energy units without converting.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: Why are two burette readings included in uncertainty?
rows.originalBack: A titre is a difference; uncertainty arises from both final and initial readings.
accept: A titre is the final reading minus the initial reading, so both readings contribute uncertainty.
reject: Only the final reading has measurement uncertainty.
Subtract the absolute uncertainty in the initial reading from the final reading uncertainty.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: How is percentage titre uncertainty found?
accept: Divide the absolute titre uncertainty by the titre and multiply by 100.
reject: Multiply the titre by its absolute uncertainty and then by 100.
Divide the titre by its absolute uncertainty and multiply by 100.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: Why can distilled water be added to the conical flask during a titration?
rows.originalBack: It changes concentration but not the number of moles being titrated.
accept: Adding distilled water dilutes the solution without changing the number of moles being titrated.
reject: Adding distilled water creates extra moles of the reactant being titrated.
Water changes the balanced reaction equation and so changes the amount being titrated.
